_about: Garden jobs for the weekly newsletter. Each rule's window runs from `from` to `to`: an anchor (a date computed for each send group in send-groups.json) plus an offset in days. Lower `order` wins when more than four jobs are due. Rules sharing a `pair` are shown together. Every heading and fact is our own wording; sources supply facts only, except US federal works, which are public domain. Read by scripts/newsletter/rules.mjs.

rules.heading: Cut back dead stems for a tidy garden
facts: Any time between your first fall frost and your last spring frost, cut dead stems to 12–24 in.
Last season's stems are still empty. Cutting them does not harm nesting bees.
Leave the stubble up so bees can nest in it next growing season.

sources.title: NC State Extension AG-984, Garden Cleanup for Pollinators: Trim Perennial Stems in Their First Winter (2025)

rules.heading: Cut stems later for a pollinator-friendly garden
facts: Leave stems and seed heads standing until daytime highs stay above 50°F.
Then cut stems to mixed heights of 8–24 in.
Leave the cuttings on the ground.
Both ways are the same for the plant because it is dormant and regrows from its roots.

rules.heading: Cut back last season's grasses
facts: Cut the old clumps down to a few inches before new green shoots start to grow.

rules.heading: Prune shrubs and vines by when they flower
facts: Plants that flower in summer bloom on new growth. Prune them now before their buds open.
Plants that flower in spring already carry their buds. Wait until their flowers fade.

sources.title: USDA Home and Garden Bulletin 165, Pruning Ornamental Shrubs and Vines (1969)
sources.license: Public domain (US federal work). Facts adapted in our own words.

sources.license: Public domain (US federal work). Facts adapted in our own words.

rules.heading: Divide crowded fall-blooming perennials
facts: Divide them around your last spring frost while they are not in flower.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension, Dividing Perennials
sources.license: © Regents of the University of Minnesota, all rights reserved. Facts only, in our own words.

rules.heading: Divide crowded perennials that flower in spring and summer
facts: Divide them in the weeks before your first fall frost.
Finish four to six weeks before the ground freezes so the roots can settle in.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension, Dividing Perennials
sources.license: © Regents of the University of Minnesota, all rights reserved. Facts only, in our own words.

rules.heading: Prune trees while they are dormant
facts: Prune now while the trees are dormant.
Wait to prune trees that flower in early spring until their flowers fade.
Do not prune oaks in spring or early summer. Fresh cuts in those months draw the beetles that spread oak wilt.

sources.title: USDA Forest Service, How to Prune Trees (NA-FR-01-95, revised 2012)

rules.heading: Plant new natives
facts: The weeks around your last spring frost are a good time to set out new plants.
Water them regularly through their first growing season.

sources.title: Plant Virginia Natives, Gardening through the Seasons

rules.heading: Plant trees and shrubs
facts: Plant them before your first fall frost.
Keep watering them as needed until the ground freezes.

rules.heading: Leave fallen leaves in your beds
facts: Rake leaves onto your beds and around shrubs instead of bagging them.
Many moths, butterflies, and bumble bee queens winter in or under them.
Keep the leaves whole. Shredding them can kill the insects inside.

rules.heading: Sow native seed that needs a cold winter
facts: Many native seeds need weeks of cold and damp weather before they will sprout.
Sow them outdoors after your first hard freeze. That way a warm spell does not sprout them too early.

rules.heading: Water new plants
facts: New plants need regular water through their first growing season.
When rain is short, give them a deep soaking.

sources.title: Plant Virginia Natives, Gardening through the Seasons

rules.heading: Pull weeds before they set seed
facts: Pulling weeds before their seeds ripen keeps them from spreading.

sources.title: Indiana Native Plant Society, Ecological Garden Maintenance
sources.license: © Indiana Native Plant Society, all rights reserved. Facts only, in our own words.

rules.heading: Mow a new meadow when it gets tall
facts: Most of what shoots up tall in a meadow's first year is weeds.
Each time it reaches 12–18 in., mow it to about 8 in.
Stop mowing as your first fall frost nears.
